title: Ahead: the great questions
hookLine: year three turns to suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness and awe, across many traditions

lines: THE QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.
cards: Some questions come up at four in the afternoon, between emails. Most don't.
The big ones come in hospital corridors, at gravesides, on the night a baby is born, in the car after you've been let go, on a mountain when the clouds suddenly open. Why is there so much suffering?
What happens when we die? Can I forgive this? Traditions all over the world have sat up late with those questions.
Tomorrow the porch closes for the year. Today, a look ahead.

teach.h: SIX QUESTIONS, ONE AT A TIME.
teach.b: First, the six. Year three is built around six questions: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, and awe. Not a new school this time, and not a single book.
Six themes, each given room, one after another. Second, how it works.
Each question gets many voices: scripture and saints, sages and poets, philosophers and scientists. Every voice is named.
A line from the Psalms is the Psalms; a teaching of the Buddha is the Buddha's; a finding from a lab is the lab's. Nobody is blended into anybody else, and nobody is ranked.
Where traditions see a question differently, and on death they really do, each says what it says, in its own words, and it's left there. Third, the porch comes too. The Stoics don't disappear.
On death there's Marcus and the ripe olive that falls blessing the tree; on awe, Marcus again, looking down from above.

teach.h: THE STOICS AT A BIGGER TABLE.
teach.b: In year three they take a seat at a much bigger table, one voice among many. Fourth, questions to live with. In 1903 the poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote to a young man who had asked him for advice.
Be patient, he told him, with what is still unsettled in you.
Love the questions themselves. Don't chase answers you aren't ready to live yet.
Live the questions now, and one day you may find, almost without noticing, that you've grown into an answer.
That's the spirit of year three: not a quiz with answers in the back, but a year of good company with the hard questions.

how: Some people on their own spiritual path return again and again to a few great questions, reading what different traditions, philosophers and scientists say about each.

games.why: that's the year-three way: every voice named, none ranked, and the question left open for you to live with.

practice: Let the six questions pass through you, one breath each: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Notice which one tugs, which one your body leans toward or flinches from.
When you've found it, let it sit beside you like a companion for the road; you don't need an answer.
